title: Processes and CPU Scheduling: Who Gets the Processor Next

questions.question: What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is a running instance; a process is a file on disk
A program is a passive file on disk; a process is that program in execution
They are two names for exactly the same thing
A process exists only after the program is uninstalled
questions.rationale: A program is a passive file of instructions; a process is a program in execution, with memory and bookkeeping state created by the OS.

questions.question: A process whose time slice just expired, and which will run again later, moves from Running to which state?
options: Waiting (blocked)
Terminated
Ready
New
questions.rationale: On preemption (time slice end or arrival of a higher-priority process) the process moves from Running back to Ready; Waiting is only for I/O or events.

questions.question: Which statement about a context switch is correct?
options: It performs useful user work while switching
It is pure overhead, since no user work happens during the switch
It happens only when a process terminates
It requires no register or state saving
questions.rationale: A context switch saves one process's state into its PCB and loads another's; it is pure overhead of typically a few microseconds, including register reloads and cache pollution.

questions.question: The convoy effect, where short jobs queue behind one long job, is a weakness of which scheduling algorithm?
options: First-come, first-served (FCFS)
Shortest job first (SJF)
Round Robin
Priority scheduling with aging
questions.rationale: In the worked example, FCFS ran P1 (burst 24) first, so P2 and P3 waited 24 and 27 ms — short jobs stuck behind a long one, like cars behind a truck.

questions.question: In the worked example (P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at 0), what average waiting time does SJF achieve?
options: 17 ms
3 ms
5.7 ms
27 ms
questions.rationale: SJF runs P2 (0–3), P3 (3–6), then P1 (6–30): waiting times are 0, 3, and 6 — an average of 3 ms, which is provably optimal for a fixed batch.

questions.question: Waiting time for a process is computed as:
options: Completion time − arrival time
Turnaround time − CPU burst
First response − arrival
Time slice × number of processes
questions.rationale: Turnaround = completion − arrival, and waiting = turnaround − burst; response time is first response − arrival.

questions.question: Which pair of problems does SJF suffer from?
options: Convoy effect and no preemption
Needing future burst lengths and possible starvation of long jobs
Excessive context switches and convoy effect
Aging and priority inversion
questions.rationale: SJF needs to know (or estimate) future burst lengths, and long jobs can starve while a stream of shorter jobs keeps arriving.

questions.question: What is the standard fix for starvation in priority scheduling?
options: Increasing the time quantum to infinity
Using FCFS as a tiebreaker only
Aging — gradually raising the priority of processes that wait too long
Removing all priorities and using SJF
questions.rationale: Aging gradually raises the priority of long-waiting processes so even the humblest job eventually runs.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes concurrency from parallelism?
options: Concurrency requires multiple cores; parallelism requires one
Concurrency is interleaved progress on one core; parallelism is simultaneous execution on several cores
They are identical concepts from different textbooks
Parallelism is only about structure, not simultaneity
questions.rationale: Concurrency is about structure — many processes make progress by interleaving on one core; parallelism is simultaneity across several cores. A single-core machine is concurrent but never parallel.

questions.question: Compared with a process, a thread is cheaper to create and communicate through because threads:
options: Have their own isolated address space
Share one address space, code, and open files with sibling threads
Run only in kernel mode
Never need locks or synchronization
questions.rationale: Threads inside one process share its address space, so creation is light and communication uses shared variables — though that shared state needs locks and reduces failure isolation.
